paras: The threatened lynching of Robert Wood was an episode in York County, South Carolina, reported in early July 1888, in which a party of about fifty white men ordered Wood, a white man of about sixty, to leave the county within five days. Wood had been charged with injuring and mutilating a six-year-old white girl, and the only report said he was supposed to have left and would be lynched or "very roughly handled" if he stayed.

According to the report, Wood was "a white man of sixty years, with a family" who was charged with "brutally injuring and mutilating" a white girl named Hill, aged six. The item called the alleged assault "a horrible crime" but did not say when or where in the county it occurred.

A party of about fifty white men went at night to the house of the girl's mother. Although she was "quite ill," they forced her to make an affidavit that Wood was the person who had injured the child. The men then notified Wood to quit the county in five days "or take the consequences."

Wood was "supposed to have gone," and the paper wrote that if he remained he would be "either lynched or very roughly handled." No report of an arrest, a trial of Wood, or any action against the party appears in the coverage, nor any confirmation of whether he left.

The only account found ran on 7 July 1888 in the Charlotte Messenger of Charlotte, North Carolina, as an unattributed paragraph in a column of South Carolina news, beside an item about a fatal bank cave-in near Rock Hill. It named no source and no members of the party, and it reported the coerced affidavit and the order to leave without comment while calling the alleged assault "a horrible crime."
